assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Viscosity
items.clue: How thick a liquid is and how easily it flows.

items.label: Combustion
items.clue: Burning a fuel in oxygen, which releases energy.

items.label: Polymer
items.clue: A very long molecule made by joining many small molecules together.

items.label: Cracking
items.clue: Breaking down hydrocarbons to produce smaller, more useful molecules.

questions.stem: Some properties of hydrocarbons depend on the size of their molecules. Which set of properties is this?

options.text: Boiling point, solubility and conductivity
Colour, density and electrical conductivity
Boiling point, viscosity and flammability
Density, hardness and melting point

questions.explanation: These are the three properties the specification names as depending on molecular size.

questions.stem: How do the properties of hydrocarbons change as the molecules get larger?

options.text: Boiling point down, viscosity up, flammability down
Boiling point rises, viscosity down, flammability up
Boiling point falls, viscosity falls, flammability up
Boiling point up, viscosity up, flammability down

questions.explanation: Larger molecules attract each other more strongly, so they boil higher and flow less easily, and they are harder to ignite.

questions.stem: How does the boiling point of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It decreases, as larger molecules are heavier and move slower
It increases, as larger molecules attract each other more strongly
It stays the same, since size only affects density
It rises at first and then falls again for long chains

questions.explanation: More energy is needed to separate larger molecules, so the boiling point rises with molecular size.

questions.stem: How does the viscosity of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It increases, so the liquid catches fire faster
It decreases, so the liquid flows freely
It increases, so the liquid flows less easily
It is the same for all liquid hydrocarbons

questions.explanation: Longer molecules attract and tangle with each other more, so thick fractions pour very slowly.

questions.stem: How does the flammability of a hydrocarbon change as its molecules get larger?

options.text: It increases, as there is more carbon to burn
It increases, so it is easier to set alight
It does not change for any hydrocarbon
It decreases, so it is harder to ignite

questions.explanation: Large molecules are hard to vaporise, and a fuel must vaporise before it will burn.

questions.stem: Liquefied petroleum gases are used in portable camping stoves. Which property makes them suitable?

options.text: They are highly flammable and ignite very easily
They have high boiling points and do not evaporate
They are very viscous and pour out slowly and safely
They contain the largest hydrocarbon molecules of all

questions.explanation: Small hydrocarbon molecules vaporise readily and are highly flammable, which is exactly what a small stove needs.

questions.stem: What happens when a hydrocarbon undergoes complete combustion?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen form, and energy is taken in
Carbon monoxide and water form, and energy is released
Carbon dioxide and water form, and heat energy is released
Carbon dioxide and water form, and energy is taken in

questions.explanation: The specification states that complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water, and that combustion releases energy.

questions.stem: During the combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel, what happens to the carbon and the hydrogen?

options.text: Only the carbon is oxidised, not the hydrogen
Both are reduced, because both lose oxygen
Only carbon dioxide forms, and no water
Both are oxidised, because both gain oxygen

questions.explanation: The carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidised to water, so both gain oxygen.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the complete combustion of methane, CH₄?

options.text: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
2CH₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 4H₂O
2CH₄ + 4O₂ → CO₂ + 4H₂O
CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O

questions.explanation: Carbon: 1 and 1. Hydrogen: 4 and 4. Oxygen: 4 and 4. The equation is balanced.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the complete combustion of propane, C₃H₈?

options.text: 2C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 6CO₂ + 8H₂O
C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
2C₃H₈ + 10O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O
2C₃H₈ + 10O₂ → 6CO₂ + 10H₂O

questions.explanation: Carbon: 3 and 3. Hydrogen: 8 and 8. Oxygen: 10 and 10. The equation is balanced.

questions.stem: Ethane has the formula C₂H₆. Which equation shows its complete combustion?

options.text: C₂H₆ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
C₂H₆ + O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
C₂H₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O

questions.explanation: Carbon: 4 and 4. Hydrogen: 12 and 12. Oxygen: 14 and 14. Doubling the ethane avoids a half-molecule of oxygen.
